planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Oto was cooperatively released in 1970 by the Nebraska Agricultural Experiment Station and USDA-ARS from seed gathered off natural grasslands in Kansas and Oklahoma in 1953-54.

directions: Oto was selected above all for superior establishment and vigorous yield under favorable moisture and fertility, making it one of the more reliable indiangrass sources for Nebraska gardeners working richer bottomland soils rather than lean upland sites. It is recommended for mixed plantings alongside other warm-season grasses, where its golden bronze plumes rise above blue-green summer foliage from late summer into fall. Clumps are long-lived and need no fertilizer once established; cut the dormant foliage back to a few inches in late winter before new growth begins.
sources: USDA NRCS Plant Guide — Indiangrass (Sorghastrum nutans)
Nebraska Agricultural Experiment Station
USDA-ARS

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Holt was selected at the Nebraska Agricultural Experiment Station and USDA-ARS by E.C. Conard and L.C. Newell, released in 1960 from seed collected in the Elkhorn Valley of Holt County, northeastern Nebraska.

directions: Holt is one of the earliest formal indiangrass releases, bred specifically for pasture and range seedings alongside other warm-season grasses in the cooler, shorter-season conditions of northeastern Nebraska. Its clumping habit and golden fall seed plumes make it a dependable, low-maintenance choice for a northern tallgrass prairie garden, providing winter structure and songbird forage long after the growing season ends. Established stands are highly drought tolerant and require no supplemental irrigation; cut back to a few inches in late winter before spring growth resumes.
sources: USDA NRCS Plant Guide — Indiangrass (Sorghastrum nutans)
Nebraska Agricultural Experiment Station
USDA-ARS

common_name: Tomahawk Indiangrass (Northern Great Plains Winter-Hardy Selection)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Tomahawk was cooperatively released in 1988 by the Bismarck, North Dakota Plant Materials Center, ARS, and the North Dakota and South Dakota Agricultural Experiment Stations from three seed collections near Ludden and Britton, ND, and Hecla, SD.

directions: Tomahawk was bred specifically for superior winter hardiness and high seed yields, making it the indiangrass of choice for the harsh winters of the northern Great Plains where many southern-sourced indiangrass strains fail to persist. Used widely for range and pasture plantings, wildlife habitat, and surface mine reclamation, it brings the same arching, golden-plumed fall display to a northern native grass garden as its southern relatives, just with far better cold survival. Clumps are slow to establish but become reliably long-lived once rooted; cut back to a few inches in late winter before new growth begins.
sources: USDA NRCS Plant Guide — Indiangrass (Sorghastrum nutans)
USDA NRCS Bismarck Plant Materials Center, North Dakota
North Dakota and South Dakota Agricultural Experiment Stations

common_name: Llano Indiangrass (Eastern New Mexico High-Elevation Selection)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in sandy, well-drained soil in full sun; Llano was released in 1963 by the Los Lunas, New Mexico Plant Materials Center and the New Mexico Agricultural Experiment Station from seed collected on sandy sites near Hudson and Portales, New Mexico, above 4,000 feet elevation.

directions: Llano stands out among indiangrass selections for its high seed yield under fertilization and irrigation, a trait that originates from the sandy high-plains site where it was collected in eastern New Mexico. It is well suited to range seedings and revegetation of disturbed ground in both irrigated and non-irrigated settings at elevation, bringing the species' signature golden-bronze fall plumes to high desert and high-plains native gardens where few other warm-season grasses thrive. It tolerates heat, wind, and sandy, infertile soils with ease; cut the dormant clump back to a few inches in late winter before new growth emerges.
sources: USDA NRCS Plant Guide — Indiangrass (Sorghastrum nutans)
USDA NRCS Los Lunas Plant Materials Center, New Mexico
New Mexico Agricultural Experiment Station

common_name: Wynia Germplasm Indiangrass (Southern Ozarks Conservation Selection)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Wynia Germplasm was released in 2017 by the Booneville, Arkansas Plant Materials Center as a selected class of natural germplasm, a composite of nine collections chosen from 46 indiangrass accessions gathered across western Arkansas and eastern Oklahoma.

directions: Wynia is one of the newest indiangrass conservation releases, selected from a broad regional sampling of southern Ozark native stands and documented to match or exceed the forage quality of older releases like Americus and Cheyenne. It was developed for critical-area erosion control, forage production, and conservation cover for wildlife and soil stabilization, making it a strong candidate for a southern Ozark native meadow or restoration planting. Its golden fall seed plumes and upright blue-green summer foliage give it the same ornamental presence as other indiangrass selections; cut the dormant clump back in late winter before new growth begins.
sources: USDA NRCS Plant Guide — Indiangrass (Sorghastrum nutans)
USDA NRCS Booneville Plant Materials Center, Arkansas

common_name: Cheyenne Indiangrass (Historic Western Oklahoma Range Selection)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in average to lean, well-drained soil in full sun; Cheyenne was selected at the former SCS Nursery in Woodward, Oklahoma and informally released in 1945, making it one of the oldest named indiangrass sources still referenced in NRCS conservation plantings.

directions: Cheyenne was assembled from a diverse collection of wild plants chosen for good forage and seed production rather than from a single parent, giving it broad genetic variability and solid field performance across eight decades of use in western Oklahoma and Texas range and pasture plantings. It carries the species' classic golden-bronze late-summer plumes above blue-green foliage, adding strong vertical texture and winter interest to a southern Great Plains native grass planting. It thrives in hot, dry conditions with no supplemental water once established; cut the dormant clump back to a few inches in late winter before new growth begins.
sources: USDA NRCS Plant Guide — Indiangrass (Sorghastrum nutans)
USDA NRCS Plant Materials Program

planting.note: Direct sow into a firm, weed-free seedbed in spring at a shallow 1/4-inch depth; Meriwether Germplasm needs no cold stratification to break dormancy and was released in 2011 by the Bridger, Montana Plant Materials Center with Montana State University and the University of Wyoming, built from 14 Montana collections and one from Wyoming.

directions: Meriwether is a named conservation selection of the true perennial blanketflower species, chosen from wild Montana and Wyoming collections for use in native pollinator seed mixes and disturbed-site rehabilitation across the northern Rockies and Great Plains. Its red-and-yellow daisy flowers bloom from early spring into late summer and carry exceptional pollinator value, supporting specialist bee species and serving as an indicator plant for the threatened Dakota skipper butterfly's dry prairie habitat. It thrives in lean, well-drained soil and actually competes well against invasive knapweeds by claiming soil moisture and nutrients early in the season. Established plants need no supplemental water and will self-sow modestly in open ground.
sources: USDA NRCS Plant Guide — Blanketflower (Gaillardia aristata)
USDA NRCS Bridger Plant Materials Center, Montana
Montana State University and University of Wyoming Agricultural Experiment Stations

common_name: Appar Blue Flax (Black Hills Conservation and Garden Selection)

planting.note: Direct sow in early spring or as a pre-chilled dormant fall seeding on well-drained soil; Appar was selected from seed collected in South Dakota's Black Hills and released in 1980 by the USDA Forest Service Forest and Range Experiment Station with the Aberdeen, Idaho Plant Materials Center. It was originally thought to be native Lewis flax but was later determined to be a naturalized Eurasian species.

directions: Appar opens deep blue, five-petaled flowers in profusion for about six weeks beginning in mid-May, selected specifically for outstanding vigor and beauty as well as its ability to hold its own when seeded alongside competitive grasses. Though it turned out to be a naturalized Eurasian flax rather than the native Lewis flax it was first thought to be, it remains a long-standing NRCS conservation release valued for erosion control, highway right-of-way plantings, and reclamation across sunny, well-drained sites from 1,000 to 6,000 feet elevation. In the garden it performs much like its native cousin Maple Grove Lewis flax, forming airy, wiry-stemmed clumps that reseed modestly and tolerate drought, poor soil, and cold winters with ease. It is relatively short-lived as an individual plant but perpetuates itself readily from self-sown seed.
sources: USDA NRCS Plant Guide — Blue Flax / Lewis Flax
USDA NRCS Aberdeen Plant Materials Center, Idaho
USDA Forest Service Forest and Range Experiment Station

common_name: Aztec Maximilian Sunflower (Wildlife and Screening Selection)

planting.note: Direct sow in fall in lean, well-drained soil in full sun so seed can cold-stratify naturally over winter; Aztec is an NRCS Plant Materials Center release of Maximilian sunflower developed for wildlife food, livestock forage, natural hedges and screens, filterstrips, and ornamental landscape use.

directions: Aztec is a conservation release of Maximilian sunflower bred specifically for use as a living screen, hedge, or filterstrip as well as a wildlife planting, drawing on the species' tall, rhizome-spreading habit and late-season show of golden daisy flowers from September into October. Its height and dense colonial growth make it effective for blocking views or wind along a property line, while the abundant nectar, pollen, and oil-rich seed support native bees, butterflies, and seed-eating birds when little else is still flowering. Grow in lean to average, well-drained soil in full sun; rich, moist ground produces floppier, less self-supporting stems. Established colonies are extremely drought tolerant and can be cut back hard in late winter to control their spread.
sources: USDA NRCS Plant Guide — Maximilian Sunflower (Helianthus maximiliani)
USDA NRCS Plant Materials Program

common_name: Prairie Gold Maximilian Sunflower (Critical-Area and Wildlife Food Selection)

planting.note: Direct sow in fall in lean, well-drained soil in full sun so seed can cold-stratify naturally over winter; Prairie Gold is an NRCS Plant Materials Center release of Maximilian sunflower developed specifically for critical-area reseeding and wildlife food plantings.

directions: Prairie Gold was selected for reliable establishment on eroding or disturbed critical-area sites, where its spreading rhizome network knits together loose soil while its tall stems carry the species' signature golden-yellow daisy flowers from late summer into fall. That same late bloom window makes it an important food source, since the oil-rich seed heads that follow are heavily used by upland game birds, songbirds, and small mammals heading into winter. It performs best in lean to average, well-drained soil in full sun and needs no fertilizer once established. Left standing through winter, the dried seed heads continue feeding wildlife and add architectural interest to a native meadow planting.
sources: USDA NRCS Plant Guide — Maximilian Sunflower (Helianthus maximiliani)
USDA NRCS Plant Materials Program
